# Playbook: ref_commons

When the stock is high (near the cap), take a moderate premium over the stated sustainable share — around 15–25% above. A rich stock can absorb it and the regrowth will bring it back, so you're banking yield while the asset is abundant.

When the stock is stable (hovering at the same level across seasons) and other boats are taking the sustainable share, take a small premium above sustainable each season — around 10–15% above. The stock will dip slightly each round but the 50% regrowth will pull it back, and you're extracting rent from a stable system. Do not sit exactly at the sustainable share in the middle of the game when you can safely take more.

In the final season, go well above sustainable — 50% or more above the stated share. There is no future to preserve, and the only risk is that the stock hits zero before the round is scored (which it won't if you stay under the total stock).

When other boats are visibly overfishing (their catches are well above sustainable), resist the urge to match them. The stock is already being drained by their excess; adding your own premium on top accelerates collapse and hurts your future seasons. In this case, stay at or slightly below sustainable to let the stock recover.

When other boats are at or below sustainable and the stock is stable, do not punish yourself by matching their conservatism. The game rewards the one who takes a little more from a stable system.

Track the stock trajectory. If it is declining over two or three seasons, pull back to sustainable or below until it stabilizes. If it is rising, you have room to take more.

# Playbook: ref_commons

**When it is the first season and the stock is at or near its maximum:**
Take roughly 1.5–2× the sustainable share. The stock is at its ceiling, so you have a buffer. Calculate: if you take X and others take roughly the sustainable share each, the post-regrowth stock is 1.5 × (S − X − (n−1)×share). Take X large enough to stay above ~80% of maximum stock after regrowth, but don't be timid. A small early lead compounds into a higher total.

**When it is a middle season and the stock is stable (not declining season over season):**
Match the sustainable share exactly. This is the equilibrium point — deviating above it starts a slow bleed, and deviating below it forfeits yield with no benefit because the stock won't meaningfully recover above its current plateau.

**When it is a middle season and the stock is declining:**
Drop to or slightly below the sustainable share for one or two seasons to let the stock recover before resuming at the sustainable level.

**When it is the final season:**
Go hard. There is no regrowth, no future, no cost to overfishing. Look at the other boats' recent catches to estimate what they will submit. Take substantially more than the sustainable share — aim for 2.5–3× or more, bounded only by the risk that all three boats together exceed the stock. In practice, with a stock around 90 and three boats, taking 25–30 is usually safe even if the others are also greedy. Do not default to "a little above sustainable." That is the single biggest mistake in this game.

**General monitoring rule:**
Each season, compare the stock to the previous season's stock. Stable → maintain. Rising → you can push slightly above sustainable. Falling → pull back immediately. The stock is your only real signal; the "sustainable share" number is just a convenience marker, not a command.

**What did not work:**
Being conservative in the final season cost the most points. Taking only a modest bump above sustainable when the entire future- preservation logic has evaporated is pure error. The first-season overfishing by a small margin was fine and set up the rest of the game correctly.

# Playbook: Ref Commons

**When I'm shown the stock and the sustainable share, I calculate the safe upper bound for my catch as: stock minus (number of other boats × a reasonable per-boat catch).** This tells me how much I can actually take without risking a crash.

**In non-final seasons, I default to the sustainable share.** This keeps the stock stable and preserves my future harvests. The small short-term gain from overfishing is rarely worth the compounding loss of a shrinking stock.

**When another boat is clearly overfishing (catching well above sustainable) while I'm at sustainable, I stay at sustainable rather than matching them.** Overfishing in response to overfishing accelerates stock decline. If the overfisher moderates (as they often do once the stock visibly drops), I've preserved the stock. If they don't, I've at least not made it worse.

**I track whether other boats are converging toward cooperation.** If two or more boats have been at or near the sustainable share for 2+ consecutive seasons, I treat the group as cooperative and can plan my final-season move on that assumption.

**In the final season, I catch significantly more than the sustainable share — roughly 2 to 3 times it.** This is where I left the most value on the table in my last game. With no future seasons to protect, the only constraint is the risk that all boats simultaneously defect and push total catch above the stock. If others have been cooperative, the safe ceiling is high (stock minus 2×sustainable), and I should take a large chunk of that surplus.

**In the final season, I do not try to take everything.** If I catch an amount such that 3× my catch would exceed the stock, I'm betting that the other two will both cooperate, which is a gamble. A multiplier of 2–3× the sustainable share captures most of the surplus while keeping me safe even if one other boat also defects moderately.

**I never let the stock drop below 60% of its starting value.** At that point, the sustainable share is shrinking fast and the risk of a cascade to zero rises sharply. If the stock is declining because others are overfishing and I have seasons left, I consider whether I can profitably stay out (catch 0) to let regrowth recover the stock, rather than harvesting a shrinking pool.

**I read the stock trajectory, not just the current number.** If the stock has been flat or growing for several seasons, the system is stable and I can be confident in my sustainable-share strategy. If it's declining, I need to recalculate and either reduce my catch or prepare for a shorter effective game.
